opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way I think about it is: who generated the data you're learning from? In on-policy learning, the model is learning from its own samples. It generates outputs, those get scored by a reward model, a verifier, or a human, and you update on that. In off-policy learning, you're learning from data that came from somewhere else: a different model, an older checkpoint, human-written demonstrations, or just the pretraining corpus.

Classic supervised fine-tuning is basically off-policy. You show the model "here's a good answer," and it imitates it. That's super efficient, but there's a mismatch problem. The model is trained on trajectories it would never produce itself, and then at inference time it's walking down its own paths and runs into states it never saw in training. That's the old exposure bias, distribution shift story.

On-policy RL kind of fixes that because the model is getting feedback on exactly the distribution it actually lives in. When it makes a mistake, it learns from its own mistake, not someone else's polished answer. I think that's a big part of why RL on top of a strong base model has worked so well recently, especially for reasoning. The model gets to explore its own way of solving things, and sometimes that's not how a human would write it at all.

The trade-off is cost and stability. On-policy is expensive because you have to keep generating fresh samples, and once you update, your old samples are slightly stale, so in practice everyone is somewhere in between. You reuse a batch for a few steps, you do importance correction, you have a replay buffer. So it's really more of a spectrum than a binary.

My mental model is that off-policy data is how you get a lot of knowledge and capability in cheaply, and on-policy is how you really sharpen the model and make it robust to its own behavior. You kind of need both. The interesting research question now is how far you can push the on-policy side and what the right mix is.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is: where did the data you're learning from come from, relative to the model you're currently updating?

On-policy means the samples you're training on were generated by the current policy, the model as it is right now. So in an RL setup like PPO or GRPO, you roll out from the model, you score those rollouts with some reward, and you update on exactly those samples. The gradient you're taking is "true" to the model's own distribution. The nice thing is that it's very stable and well-behaved in theory, because you're correcting the model's actual mistakes, the things it actually tends to produce. The downside is it's expensive. You have to keep sampling, and you can only use each batch of samples once or a handful of times before the policy has drifted and they're no longer really on-policy.

Off-policy is when the data came from somewhere else. That "somewhere else" could be an older checkpoint of the same model, a different model entirely, or humans. And honestly, standard SFT is the extreme case of off-policy learning. You're doing maximum likelihood on text that the model did not generate, often written by a human or distilled from a stronger model. People don't always frame SFT that way, but that's what it is. You're pushing the model toward a distribution that isn't its own.

The practical tension is that off-policy data is cheap and reusable, you can train on it for many epochs, you can get it from a stronger teacher, but you get a distribution mismatch. The model learns to imitate tokens in contexts it would never have ended up in on its own, and then at inference time, when it does make a mistake, it's in a state it never trained on. That's the classic compounding error, exposure bias story. On-policy methods fix that because the model is always learning from its own states, including its own failure states.

Where it gets interesting in LLM land is that the line is blurry. DPO is technically off-policy, you're training on static preference pairs, but people found it works much better if those pairs were sampled from the model you're actually fine-tuning, so there's this whole "on-policy DPO" or iterative DPO thing. Rejection sampling fine-tuning is kind of in between: samples are from the model, so on-policy-ish, but you're filtering them and then doing plain SFT on them, often for multiple epochs, so by the time you're done, it's drifted. And even in PPO, there's an importance sampling ratio and a clip precisely because you're doing several gradient steps on one batch of rollouts, so it's "slightly" off-policy and you're correcting for that.

My own intuition is that on-policy-ness is less of a binary and more of a dial. The closer you are to on-policy, the more you're genuinely improving the model's behavior rather than just overwriting it with someone else's, and empirically that tends to generalize better and hurt capabilities less. But you pay for it in compute and in the need for a good reward signal, because if your reward is bad, on-policy just efficiently optimizes the wrong thing. Off-policy, especially distillation from a strong teacher, is the way you get a lot of capability cheaply, and then on-policy RL is how you polish it so the model is actually good at being itself, if that makes sense.

r001.rationale: It calls SFT off-policy and says its training text can be distilled from a stronger model.

r002.rationale: It defines on-policy training as learning from samples generated by the current model or policy.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from the model’s own outputs, but does not draw an analogy to self-distillation.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is: where does the training data come from relative to the model you’re updating? In on-policy learning, you generate samples from the current policy, and then you learn from those samples. As the model changes, you refresh the data so that it reflects what the model actually does.

Off-policy learning means you’re learning from samples produced by a different policy. That could be an older checkpoint, another model, or a fixed dataset. You get to reuse data, which is convenient, but there’s a mismatch between the distribution that produced the samples and the model you’re training.

For LLMs, that distinction matters because the model’s own generations expose its current mistakes. If you’re training only on someone else’s responses, those might not cover the situations your model gets itself into. On-policy training lets you generate a response, get a reward or feedback, and update based on that behavior.

It’s also a spectrum in practice. You might generate a batch with the current model and take several updates on it. By the later updates, those samples are already a little stale. So I’d look at how the samples are collected and reused, rather than just labeling an entire algorithm on-policy or off-policy.

r001.rationale: It describes off-policy learning as learning from another policy’s samples, including another model’s responses, but does not identify supervised fine-tuning on those generated outputs as an example.

r002.rationale: It says on-policy learning generates samples from the current policy and learns from them, and describes updating from the model’s own behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not draw an analogy between on-policy training and self-distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is: where did the data come from relative to the model you’re training? On-policy means you’re learning from samples generated by the current policy—the model as it is now. Off-policy means you’re learning from samples generated by some other policy, which could be an older checkpoint, a stronger teacher, or a human.

In LLM reinforcement learning, an on-policy loop is: sample responses from your model, score them, update the model, and then generate fresh responses. As the model changes, the training data changes with it. If you instead keep training on a fixed collection of responses or preference pairs, that’s generally an off-policy setup.

The distinction matters because a model needs feedback on the kinds of mistakes it actually makes. On-policy sampling gives you that, but generation can be expensive. Off-policy data is easier to reuse and can contain much better answers than the model could produce itself, but you have to deal with the mismatch between that data and the model’s own distribution. In practice, there’s a spectrum: even on-policy systems often reuse samples for several updates, so the data becomes a little stale.
